title_en: The Final Illness of the Prophet ﷺ
summary: In Safar of 11 AH, the Prophet ﷺ began experiencing the severe headache and fever that would be his final illness. He spent approximately fourteen days progressively weakening, led prayer for as long as he was able, and in his last days appointed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ to lead the prayers. He gave final counsel to his community and bade them farewell in the mosque.
narrative:
Aisha ؓ narrates — in accounts preserved across Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — that the Prophet ﷺ first complained of severe headache and high fever around the time he visited the Baqi al-Gharqad cemetery at night to pray for its inhabitants. He returned and told her that his head was painful. She said her own head hurt, and he smiled and said that even if she were to die before him, he would wash her, shroud her, pray over her, and bury her. She said he used to say in the time before this illness: 'Would that I knew which of my family would be the one of them to dip his hands in the henna and weep for me' — and she understood this as a premonition.

The illness intensified. Because the Prophet ﷺ alternated his nights among the houses of his wives, he asked their permission to be nursed in Aisha's room ؓ, and they agreed. For the remainder of his illness, he stayed with her. Ibn Hisham records that he was so weakened by fever that he had to lean on two men when walking to the mosque — at different stages on Ali ibn Abi Talib ؓ and on others.

For as long as he was able, the Prophet ﷺ led the prayers himself. As the illness deepened and he could no longer stand unsupported, he sent word for Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ to lead the people in prayer. Aisha ؓ initially tried to suggest Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ instead, aware of Abu Bakr's tender heart and fearing he would weep so much the congregation could not hear him. The Prophet ﷺ persisted, saying: 'Order Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer.' Al-Tabari records the count of prayers Abu Bakr led during the Prophet's illness at seventeen.

On what turned out to be one of his last Sundays, the Prophet ﷺ appeared at the mosque during Fajr prayer as Abu Bakr led the congregation. Abu Bakr moved aside upon seeing him, but the Prophet ﷺ gestured for him to stay. He sat beside Abu Bakr and prayed sitting. Al-Tabari and Ibn Hisham both preserve the companions' description of the joy and relief that swept through the congregation at the sight of him — many wept openly. Anas ibn Malik ؓ said he had never seen a more beautiful or luminous face than the Prophet's ﷺ on that morning.

In his final days, the Prophet ﷺ addressed the community from the mimbar, saying: 'Allah gave a servant the choice between this world and what Allah has for him, and the servant chose what Allah has.' Abu Bakr ؓ understood the meaning and wept, saying: 'Rather our fathers and mothers and children be ransomed for you!' The companions were puzzled at his weeping, not yet grasping that the Prophet ﷺ was speaking of himself.

Ibn Kathir preserves a report that in the final days, the Prophet ﷺ freed all his slaves and gave away whatever remained of his property. He gave repeated counsel: 'Prayer, prayer, and those whom your right hands possess' — meaning: guard your prayers and treat your dependants well. He also said: 'Do not take my grave as an object of worship.' He warned against the practices of Jews and Christians who had built places of worship over the graves of their prophets.

He asked if he owed anyone anything, and a companion said the Prophet ﷺ owed him three dirhams from a previous gift he had made to a beggar at the man's request; the Prophet ﷺ had it repaid immediately. He asked repeatedly if he had wronged anyone, so that he might make restitution before meeting Allah. These final acts of scrupulous honesty and care characterised his last conscious days.
